fix: Trust the mobile app's origin in Better Auth

<!-- claude-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"mattdy"} -->
_Requested by **Matt** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_01Qen77EXBHmef7Q9vepAedn?thread=cmsg_01Qen77EXBHmef7Q9vepAednXZgsHCk5fEewf8CykgKeNC)_

## Summary

Part 1 of 2 for #1223. The backend now trusts the mobile app's `cellarboss://` scheme as an auth origin, alongside the `CORS` list. The app PR stacked on this one moves the Android app to the Better Auth Expo client, which identifies itself by that scheme, so users no longer need to add the backend's own address to `CORS`.

## Changes

- `apps/backend/src/utils/auth.ts`: build Better Auth's `trustedOrigins` from `CORS` (trimmed, empty entries dropped) plus `MOBILE_APP_ORIGIN = "cellarboss://"`.
- `apps/backend/src/tests/auth-origin.test.ts`: unit tests for the origin list, and sign-in tests against Better Auth's real origin middleware. The scheme and the CORS origin are accepted, while an untrusted origin, an address not in `CORS`, a different custom scheme, and a cookie with no origin are all rejected.
- Docs: `CORS` and the mobile origin in `docs/backend.md`, and the comma-separated `CORS` form in the web install guide.

Browsers can't send a custom-scheme origin, so CSRF protection for the web frontend is unchanged. The `cors()` middleware is untouched.

I didn't use the `@better-auth/expo` server plugin. Its optional peer dependencies resolve to the mobile app's Expo packages in this workspace, which put Expo and React Native into `pnpm --filter backend deploy` and took the backend's `node_modules` from 627 MB to 1.1 GB. The plugin's only relevant job is copying an `expo-origin` header into `Origin`, and the app PR sets `Origin` directly instead.

This is backward compatible. Existing app versions still work with the `CORS` workaround.

- [ ] Docs / config only

## Areas affected

fix(domain): read author literals and stated counts in one pass

## What and why

Two patterns in `packages/domain` took more than linear time on text that a release controls (GHSA-9c65-xq85-phjc).

- **`parseAuthor`** split `"Name <email>"` with a pattern whose leading whitespace, lazy name and trailing whitespace could each take the same spaces. A literal with a long run of whitespace and no address took time cubic in that run. Every author name goes through it: when a deck is read, when its provenance is shown, and when the Studio starts a draft. The name comes from any release's `foaf:name` or `dcterms:creator`, which no shape limits in length, so one release could stall the tab each time its deck was shown. The literal is now trimmed and split at its last `<` when it ends in `>`, and the address is checked with a pattern that has a single way to match. The results are the same as the old pattern's for every literal, and a test compares the two on every short literal of the characters that matter.
- **Stated counts** in a making's comment ("17 chapters", "1,398 sources") were read with patterns that could begin a count at any digit after a comma. That rescanned a long run of digits and commas from each digit, quadratic in the run. A count now begins only where its run begins. The only difference: a run right after a letter, such as "a1,5 chapters", no longer reads as five.

A length limit on the name in the shapes was weighed and not made. It would change the data contract, and isn't needed once the reading is linear.

Refs: GHSA-9c65-xq85-phjc

fix(lint): run the ltex image as its own user

The ltex pre-push hook failed locally with `Permission denied` on `/usr/local/bin/ltex-cli-plus`. The image installs under a 0700 `/opt` owned by uid 1001, so the `--user $(id -u):$(id -g)` mapping can't read the binary. CI runs the image directly, which is why it never saw this.

The script now runs the container as the image's own user, with the checkout mounted read-only. LTeX only reads, so root can't leave root-owned files behind. Verified: `scripts/lint-ltex.sh` exits 0 on a clean checkout, no `LEFTHOOK_EXCLUDE`.

Closes #401

 # on PATH. Anywhere else the same image runs through Docker, which beats every

 #
+# The container runs as the image's own user (root here), not the caller's: the
+# image keeps its install under a 0700 /opt owned by uid 1001, so any other
+# `--user` mapping gets "Permission denied" on the binary. The mount is read-only
+# because LTeX only reads, which also means root can't leave root-owned files in
+# the checkout.
+#
 # ltex-cli-plus exits 3 on findings, not 1; this script passes whatever code it
 # gets straight through, so any non-zero fails the caller.
 #
@@ -28,7 +34,7 @@ if command -v ltex-cli-plus >/dev/null 2>&1; then
 fi

-  exec docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD":/work -w /work "$IMAGE" "$@"
+  exec docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/work:ro -w /work "$IMAGE" "$@"
 fi

## What I did

The `storybook:svelte-csf` Vite plugin in `@storybook/svelte-vite` resolves the runtime stories import (`@storybook/svelte/internal/svelte-csf/create-runtime-stories`) to the file inside the installed `@storybook/svelte` package. That path comes from Node's `fileURLToPath`, which keeps backslash separators on Windows. Vite expects resolved ids to use forward slashes on every OS, so on Windows a backslash id can address the runtime module a second time: its module-level setup re-runs, and the dev server can follow with a reload.

The plugin now returns the path through Vite's `normalizePath`, which rewrites separators on Windows and leaves POSIX paths unchanged. The `resolveId` unit test pins the contract by mocking the runtime path as a Windows-style literal and asserting the id comes back with forward slashes. Because Vite's `normalizePath` only rewrites separators when the process itself runs on Windows, the test stubs it to that documented id contract, keeping the suite deterministic on any OS.

POSIX projects resolve through the same code path as before; no other behavior changes.
